works.title: Wave Universe Theory (TUO): From the Electromagnetic Origin of the Vacuum to the Covariant Reformulation of Gravity and Cosmology
key_claims: This repository presents two fundamental works establishing the theoretical framework of the Wave Universe Theory (TUO), a novel unified approach to vacuum physics and gravitation.

The first article — *"Classical Formalisms and Correspondence with the TUO: From Maxwell and Einstein to the Vacuum Tension Field Tv"* — establishes the mathematical structure of the TUO by introducing the scalar Vacuum Tension Field (Tv).
The dynamics of Tv are derived from a covariant Lagrangian (L_TUO), allowing the deduction of field equations via the principle of least action.
The second article — *"From Confined Electromagnetic Field to Cosmic Vacuum Tension: A Bridge between Michaud's Theory and the TUO?"* — provides the physical foundation for the Tv field.
It proposes that vacuum tension is not an arbitrary fundamental field, but the macroscopic, homogenized result of the internal electromagnetic (EM) energy of elementary particles (Michaud's model).

works.title: "A Universe Without Dark Matter?"
key_claims: *By Gabriel Chardin (CNRS), originally published 4 June 2018 in Le Journal du CNRS, "Carnets de science" No.

Accepting the existence of a dark sector so pervasive as it is elusive remains, for a majority of physicists, the most obvious way to render the totality of astrophysical data at their disposal compatible with the theory of general relativity.
Without calling it a crisis, this situation is deeply frustrating for a discipline whose objective is to arrive at a theory exhaustively describing the content of our Universe and its evolution.
But for what reasons has the scientific community come to consider the existence of a dark sector as necessary?
And what are the reasons that today drive a growing number of researchers to consider alternative hypotheses?
